title: Breaking And Entering: Beverly Glenn-Copeland On Music And Re-discovery
summary: Underground icon Beverly Glenn-Copeland has had an extraordinary career spanning over 40 years. He joins Simon and Lauren to reflect on his new retrospective compilation, Transmissions: The Music Of Beverly Glenn-Copeland. Drawing on Buddhist thought, he says that the music that connects most with others was often created beyond his abilities as an artist and he believes that it was transmitted to him by a higher means he labels the “universal broadcasting system”.
transcript:
In an interview broadcast on Breaking and Entering on 26 November 2020, Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler spoke with singer, composer and transgender activist Beverly Glenn-Copeland about his retrospective Transmissions: The Music of Beverly Glenn-Copeland and the documentary Keyboard Fantasies. Glenn, then in his mid-seventies, had spent fifty years recording music that combined technology, spirituality and place, while writing plays and soundtracks, appearing on Mr. Dressup for almost thirty years and writing for Sesame Street. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: The documentary Keyboard Fantasies is screening at film festivals, and an artist who has long championed Glenn's music, Caribou, asks, 'How could music this beautiful have been forgotten for so long?' These records weren't collectors' favourites or rare gems; nobody had access to them. The story of how Ryota Masuko of SHE Ye,Ye Records emailed Glenn and introduced Keyboard Fantasies to a whole new generation is extraordinary. We began our interview by asking what it's been like for him to know that these songs are having such an impact after all this time.

Glenn: Oh my goodness, what a leading question. What is that like? It was not anything I ever expected. That's the first thing. Which is not to say that I didn't try to get the music out, because I did. Why have music that you're not going to share? It was obvious very quickly, at the point where I started to record, which was in 1970, that the music could not find an audience with ease because I didn't fit into any easily identifiable category. It wasn't folk music, rock and roll, blues or jazz. It mostly wasn't.

Glenn: The companies, even with the first couple of albums, didn't know where to put it on the shelf in the record store. People couldn't find it even if they wanted to, because the stores just didn't know what to do with it. Very quickly I realised that though I was writing things, and was able to record a few things in the early days, there wasn't an audience for it. I did a little touring, but not a lot. Certainly after 1980, I no longer attempted to do concerts, and I didn't concern myself with anything other than writing. All that to say that I had no expectations, really. When Ryota Masuko got in touch with me, I was stunned. Not so stunned that he found me, although that in itself was enough. But when he sold thirty records, or thirty cassettes, in a day and a half or something like that, that was beyond. I had barely sold thirty in the whole time I'd had them. Then he wanted to sell that many more. I wasn't tuned in at all to what was going on in the music world. I was a person who lived in silence, essentially. I might as well have been a monk as far as music was concerned. I didn't know that he had an international presence via the internet, but he did. As a result, it kick-started something. He was able to reach all these young people who weren't born when Keyboard Fantasies was being written, or were just being born. All of a sudden there was this audience, and I was, quite frankly, stunned. That's the best way to put it. Just plain stunned, but happy. Happy stunned.

Simon: Transmissions: The Music of Beverly Glenn-Copeland contains music from different periods of your life, revealing the diversity of your interests. For many people, it's a chance to discover your music. Has it been a chance for you to rediscover yourself at various points in your life?

Glenn: Oh yeah, totally. Because I never listen to any music. Once I've written something, I never listen to it again. It's strange, but that's just the way it is. I'm always in the moment. Many of those pieces I literally hadn't heard in thirty or forty years. To have things from all these different times of my life, it was an awakening to hear it and understand that, with a few exceptions, the things I'd been exploring were things that young people related to. When I heard it, I had to develop a relationship with it again. It was very interesting. There was a piece on that album, 'Colour of Anyhow'. I didn't relate to that piece at all because it was a love song. I'd stopped writing love songs literally in 1980 or something. When I went back, young people wanted to hear it because it related to the time of life they were in as well. At first I didn't want to sing it. It didn't make any sense to me. But I thought, they want to hear it, and I must be generous. Who am I to say, no, sorry? So I started singing it and discovered a relationship with it that I didn't have when I was young. I sing it differently than I did then. Even though the notes are still the same, the feeling inside is quite different. It's been a chance to re-establish relationships with things and experience them from my age now of seventy-six, as opposed to thirty when I wrote it, or twenty-eight, or whatever I was.

Lauren: Transmissions begins with 'La Vita', or 'The Life', originally from Primal Prayer, released in 2004. You weren't involved in determining the order of the songs, but could you tell us more about this song, particularly some of the lyrics?

Glenn: I love 'La Vita'. It's so real. It was a time when I was willing to talk about the difficulties of life, the challenges. You're moving so fast and trying to get it all together, and you don't know. You need to be more of this, opening this and opening that, and on and on. There's this anxiety about it. It's an anxious piece. At first, from the get-go, it goes into this incredible thing, but then I start yakking about the anxiety of life. Then it goes back to me singing what I consider a very beautiful classical melody. I seriously love that melody. The woman singing it is one of the most extraordinary singers I've ever heard in my life, and she happened to be a very dear friend of mine. So it goes back to that, with me singing it with her. Then it culminates with the words my mother said to me in the last twenty years of her life. She lived with me, died in my arms, and we were very close in the last part of my life, or her life, approximately twenty years or so. Every once in a while, she'd say, 'Oh darling, enjoy your life.' I know she meant it in the deepest spiritual way, because life isn't all good times and everything's hunky-dory. Life is what we all know it is. It's full of wonderful things, full of pain, you name it. It's a real drama. What I really experienced from what she was saying was: I want you to be able to reflect on your life as having been a joyous thing, to have had a life. Ultimately, the joy of having experienced life is the ultimate thing.

Lauren: You mentioned that 'La Vita' arrived to you and was written in just a day. You've said, 'The music comes to me. I can't say I have a plan to write it. The bigger question for me is how it can be used as a vehicle for encouraging heart and courage.' Could you elaborate on that?

Glenn: I feel music is given to me, literally transmitted to me. In my everyday consciousness, I think about wonderful things and blah, blah, blah. But when I sit down, I don't sit down to write. I sit down to practise, because you have to maintain your craft and advance it as best you can. Then all of a sudden something comes. Not all the time. Sometimes I'm washing dishes and something comes through, or I wake from a dream, or I'm vacuuming the house. I race to put it down. When I've finished, what I've experienced is very encouraging. The bottom line of all of it that gets transmitted to me is extremely encouraging. I call it the Universal Broadcasting System. I believe this system is broadcasting to all of us all the time. In my particular case, maybe because I was doing art, or maybe I was more open, who knows? I don't know. For some reason I started to understand it, mostly because when something amazing would start to be written, after I put it down and looked at it, I'd realise it was beyond my capabilities to have written that, quite literally. Often I could barely play it back. I'd look at it and think, wow, go to that chord? After a while, I started to realise, okay, this stuff is just being sent through. Not everything I've written was sent through, of course not, but the things that have the most connection to other people's hearts and lives, and my own heart and life, have been sent through.

Lauren: I've been thinking about where ideas come from and reading that your brain is most receptive to creative ideas when it's in a state of rest. Do you think that might have something to do with it, when your brain isn't over-functioning, when you're doing the dishes?

Glenn: Yes, because the part of the brain that's the planner and the doer isn't receptive. The other part is what we more or less call the left brain, I mean the right brain. I don't even know, because now they're starting to understand that the brain works in miraculous ways. It's not such a simple thing as the left brain and the right brain. We keep learning stuff. Whatever it is that's our deepest ability to create, I really believe it comes from a more receptive state. The people I've taught, who I'm in touch with, all say the same thing. It doesn't matter whether you're a builder, mathematician, teacher or homemaker. When we relax, and in our society we rarely relax, we're on the treadmill, moving all the time. It's become a society on a world level, for the most part, except for some Indigenous people around the world who still manage to maintain some connection to timelessness. By and large, the rest of us live in this very structured, today I must accomplish this, and the list gets longer over the years of what you're supposed to accomplish in a day. We don't have time to see, hear or listen. We don't really see, hear, feel or taste. All those things get lost in the shuffle.

Simon: Your music is reaching so many people. In the documentary Keyboard Fantasies and elsewhere, people have spoken about its impact. Caribou, Daniel Snaith, said he heard a way of taking difficult things and making something positive, affirming, reassuring and comforting out of them, which is what he tries to find in his own music. He also described your limitless positivity and optimism, and enthusiasm for youth and what music can do to change the world. How do you respond to those words?

Glenn: I feel like the reason for my existence in this world is now complete. That's what I feel. I'm not saying I'm the only person saying or doing this. There are so many of us. But what the world needs right now is hope, especially because what we've done to the earth is so tragic, and the earth is suffering so much. It's easy when you look at what's going on, with the seas rising, the poles melting, the changes in the weather, the suffering of animals and all the ones that are gone because we didn't take care of the places they need to live. Or we wiped them out, or thought of them as things to make money off. However we've done this thing where money has been our god, it has created a world where all of us are in pain, even if we don't recognise it. On a subconscious level, you cannot not be in pain about what's happening. If you're in pain, what do you need most? You need to feel your pain can count for something positive, that you can turn it into action, come out of the pain of pain and into a place of, okay, what can I do? How can I respond? How can we respond? How can we change it? If we made it like this, we have the capacity to change it.

Glenn: This is a deep Buddhist perspective, and I'm sure it's a perspective in most of our deepest philosophies and religious practices. This has been proven. There's a Japanese gentleman who's a scientist, and he did very famous studies. All you have to do is look up thoughts and the crystallisation of water. He did these tests where, based on what people were thinking, ordinary water would form different crystals. If they were in a positive state and a loving space, the water would form absolutely beautiful crystals. If they were in the opposite space, the crystals were disfigured and horrible. What it proves is that we and our environment are one. If we're projecting positive things, the world literally responds to those positive things and changes. If we're putting out negative things, the world, trees, animals and water itself respond to our negativity and decline in their ability to be sustenance, and to be glorious. That has now been proven. That's an ancient Buddhist concept I've been studying for forty-eight years, that myself and my environment are one. Therefore, on a human level, if enough of us, all the billions of us, can come to a place where we feel positive, our world itself will respond and begin to heal itself.

Lauren: Thank you so much for talking to us, Glenn. There's so much to talk about, and hopefully one day we'll get to speak in person. When things open back up, would you consider coming to Australia?

Glenn: I know I'm going to have to travel once again, and if things calm down, I will. Performing isn't my first thing, and I'm getting to the age, actually I'm past the age, where touring is very physically demanding on old bones. It's just what it is. I know I won't be able to do it for very much longer, but I'd really like to come to Australia. I really would, and I look forward to that. I have one thing I'd like to add.

Glenn: I'd appreciate it if you'd be willing to put in my thank you to my wife. I'd like to thank my wife, Elizabeth Glenn-Copeland, who has been more present, more willing to suffer with me, who has at times been the only person who could make money in our family. She has been the most profound, loving, supportive partner a person could ever hope to have. I'm eternally grateful for everything she has given that has allowed me to do what I'm doing now.
